title: Ecosystems, Energy and Cycles
bigQuestion: How do energy and matter move through a living community, and what keeps its populations in check?

story.title: The Wolves Come Home to Yellowstone
story.kicker: For seventy years the park had no wolves. Then, in the winter of 1995, a truck pulled up with fourteen of them.
paragraphs: Yellowstone National Park sits mostly in Wyoming, a high plateau of geysers, forests and wide grassy valleys. In the early 1900s, park rangers shot, trapped and poisoned the wolves there, because people saw wolves as vermin that killed elk and cattle. By 1926 the last known Yellowstone wolf pack was gone. For nearly seventy years the park's largest hunter was missing.

Without wolves, the elk did well. Their numbers on the park's northern range climbed into the tens of thousands. In winter the herds crowded along the rivers and ate young willow, aspen and cottonwood shoots down to stubs. Streambanks that had once been thick with brush turned bare. Biologists argued about what was cause and what was effect, but everyone agreed the valleys looked different from the old photographs.

In January 1995, after years of debate, lawsuits and public meetings, biologists trucked fourteen gray wolves from Canada into the park and held them for a few weeks in fenced pens so they would not simply run home. Then they opened the gates. Seventeen more wolves came the next year. Within a decade there were more than a hundred wolves in Yellowstone.

The elk changed first. Their numbers on the northern range fell by more than half over the next fifteen years, partly from wolf kills, partly from hunting outside the park, drought and other predators such as cougars and grizzly bears. Where willows had been chewed to the ground, some stands grew tall again. Beavers, which eat willow and build dams from it, returned to streams they had left. Songbirds nested in the new brush.

A famous video later claimed that the wolves changed the rivers themselves. Scientists who work in the park are more careful. Some willow patches recovered and some did not; drought, beaver dams and the height of the water table all mattered too. The honest story is less tidy but more interesting: pull one thread in a living community, and many others move, though not always in the way you expect.
story.think: If you could remove or add one species to a park near you, what changes would you predict, and how would you check whether you were right?

lessons.title: How Populations Grow
lessons.mainIdea: A population grows when births plus arrivals outnumber deaths plus departures, and it can grow very fast when nothing holds it back.
reading: Put a few bacteria in a warm flask of sugar water and check back every twenty minutes. One cell becomes two, two become four, four become eight. After ten hours, if nothing slowed them down, a single cell could have become more than a billion. This kind of growth is called *exponential* growth: the more individuals there are, the more new ones are born, so the population grows faster and faster.

A *population* is all the members of one species living in one place at one time: the white-tailed deer in a county forest preserve, the dandelions in a schoolyard, the bacteria in that flask. Four things change its size. Births and immigration (animals moving in) add to it. Deaths and emigration (animals moving out) subtract from it. When the additions outnumber the subtractions, the population grows.

Exponential growth never lasts long in the real world. The bacteria run out of sugar and poison themselves with waste. Deer run out of winter browse. But for a short time, in a new place with plenty of resources, almost any living thing can grow this way. Rabbits released in Australia in 1859 spread across the continent in a few decades. A new virus in a crowded city can double its cases in days.

Ecologists draw population size on a graph with time along the bottom. Exponential growth makes a *J-shaped curve*: flat at first, then curving sharply upward. When you see that shape, you know something is growing with nothing yet holding it back, and you should ask what will eventually stop it.

words.d: all the members of one species living in the same place at the same time
growth that speeds up as the population gets bigger, because more individuals produce more offspring
the graph shape of exponential growth: flat at first, then curving sharply upward

look.title: Doubling in a Flask
look.cite: calculated from a standard 20-minute doubling time
look.prompt: Between which two rows does the population add the most cells? Why does the same doubling rule add more and more each time?

check.q: Which two things add individuals to a population?
choices: Births and immigration
Births and emigration
Deaths and immigration
Deaths and emigration
check.why: Births add new members and immigration brings members in from elsewhere. Deaths and emigration remove members.

check.q: Why does an exponentially growing population add more individuals each hour than the hour before?
choices: Each individual reproduces faster as time passes
There are more individuals reproducing, so more offspring are added
Resources become more plentiful over time
Predators stop hunting once a population is large
check.why: The per-individual rate stays the same, but a bigger population has more reproducing members, so the total added keeps rising.

check.q: A graph of a population rises slowly, then curves sharply upward. What does this shape tell you?
choices: The population has reached its limit
The population is shrinking
The population is growing with little yet holding it back
The population is being hunted heavily
check.why: A J-shaped curve is the sign of exponential growth, which happens only when resources are not yet limiting.

lessons.title: Limiting Factors and Carrying Capacity
lessons.mainIdea: Every environment can support only so many of a species, and the resources or dangers that set that limit are called limiting factors.
reading: Picture a small pond with a pair of ducks. Each spring more ducklings hatch than the pond can feed. Some starve, some are eaten by snapping turtles, some fly off to find another pond. Year after year the number of ducks hovers around the same level. That level is the pond's *carrying capacity*: the largest population of a species that a place can support over time.

What sets the limit? Ecologists call the answers *limiting factors*. Some depend on how crowded the population already is: food, water, nesting space, disease that spreads faster in crowds, and predators that gather where prey is thick. These are *density-dependent* factors, and they push harder as the population grows. That pushback is what bends a J-shaped curve over and flattens it.

Other limits do not care how many individuals there are. A hard freeze, a flood, a wildfire or a drought can wipe out a population whether it is large or small. These are density-independent factors. Illinois farmers know both kinds: a wet spring that drowns seedlings is density-independent, while a corn fungus that spreads from plant to plant across a packed field is density-dependent.

Carrying capacity is not a fixed number carved in stone. A wet year raises it for grass-eaters; a drought lowers it. Human actions change it too. Feeding deer in winter raises the carrying capacity of a forest preserve, at least until the deer strip the wildflowers and the forest itself begins to change.

words.d: the largest population of a species that an environment can support over time
anything, such as food, water, space, disease or weather, that keeps a population from growing larger
a limiting factor whose effect grows stronger as a population becomes more crowded

look.title: The Deer and the Forest Floor
look.text: A forest preserve outside Chicago has no wolves or cougars. Deer numbers rise for years. Visitors notice that the spring wildflowers, once thick under the oaks, are getting thinner. Young oak seedlings are rare. Then one hard winter, many thin deer are found dead. The next spring, fewer fawns are born.
look.prompt: Which limiting factors in this scene are density-dependent and which are density-independent? What has happened to the forest's carrying capacity for deer?

check.q: A population stays near the same size year after year. That size is called its
choices: exponential rate
limiting factor
growth curve
carrying capacity
check.why: Carrying capacity is the largest population a place can support over time, and populations tend to hover near it.

check.q: Which limiting factor is density-dependent?
choices: A disease that spreads faster in a crowded herd
A flood that drowns a whole field
A late frost that kills flowers
A volcanic eruption
check.why: Disease spreads faster when individuals are packed together, so its effect depends on population density.

check.q: What most likely happens to a meadow's carrying capacity for rabbits during a long drought?
choices: It stays exactly the same
It goes down because less grass grows
It goes up because predators leave
It becomes infinite
check.why: Carrying capacity depends on resources. Less rain means less grass, so fewer rabbits can be supported.

lessons.title: Reading a Growth Curve
lessons.mainIdea: A logistic growth curve is S-shaped: fast growth at first, then slowing as the population nears carrying capacity.
reading: In 1934 a Russian biologist named Georgy Gause grew single-celled organisms called paramecia in test tubes and counted them every day. The numbers rose fast for a few days, then slowed, then leveled off. Plotted on a graph, they made a stretched S. Ecologists call this *logistic growth*, and it is what exponential growth becomes once limiting factors take hold.

Read an S-curve from left to right. At the bottom left, the population is small and growth is slow simply because there are few breeders. In the middle, the curve climbs steeply; this is the closest the population gets to exponential growth. Near the top, the curve bends over and flattens as food, space and disease push back. The flat line at the top is the carrying capacity, often marked with the letter K.

Real populations rarely sit exactly on the line. Many overshoot it, crash below it, and swing back. Snowshoe hares in Canada rise and fall in a cycle of roughly ten years, and the lynx that eat them rise and fall a year or two behind. A population that shoots far past K, like reindeer set loose on a small island with no predators, can eat its food supply to nothing and collapse almost to zero.

When you see a population graph, ask three questions. Is it J-shaped or S-shaped? Where does it flatten, and what limiting factor probably caused that? And if it overshoots, what happened to the resource it depends on? Those three questions turn a line on paper into a story about a living place.

words.d: population growth that starts fast and then slows as it nears carrying capacity, making an S-shaped curve
when a population rises above its carrying capacity for a time, often followed by a crash
the letter ecologists use on a population graph to mark carrying capacity

look.title: A Yeast Population in a Flask
look.cite: illustrative values modeled on classic logistic-growth experiments
look.prompt: On which day did the population add the most new cells? What is the carrying capacity of this flask, and what probably set it?

check.q: What causes an S-shaped growth curve to flatten at the top?
choices: The population runs out of time
The graph runs out of space
Limiting factors such as food and disease push back harder as the population grows
The organisms stop wanting to reproduce
check.why: Density-dependent limiting factors slow growth more and more until births roughly equal deaths at carrying capacity.

check.q: Where on an S-curve is growth fastest?
choices: At the very start, when the population is tiny
At the top, at carrying capacity
After the population crashes
In the middle, where the curve is steepest
check.why: The steep middle section is where there are many breeders but resources are not yet scarce.

check.q: Reindeer put on a small island with no predators grow far past the island's carrying capacity. What is the most likely result?
choices: A crash after the food supply is eaten down
A permanent new, higher carrying capacity
Exponential growth forever
The reindeer learn to eat less
check.why: Overshooting K damages the resource base, so the population usually collapses afterward.

lessons.title: Producers, Consumers, Decomposers
lessons.mainIdea: Nearly all energy in an ecosystem enters through producers that capture sunlight, passes to consumers that eat, and is released by decomposers that break the dead apart.
reading: Stand in a prairie in July and feel the sun on your neck. That sunlight is the energy budget for almost everything alive around you. Grasses and wildflowers capture a small share of it through photosynthesis, using light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Organisms that make their own food this way are *producers*. On land they are mostly plants; in lakes and oceans they are mostly algae and tiny floating cells.

Everything that cannot make its own food must eat. These are *consumers*. A grasshopper chewing a leaf is a primary consumer, or herbivore. A meadowlark that eats the grasshopper is a secondary consumer. A hawk that takes the meadowlark is a tertiary consumer. Each of these feeding positions is called a *trophic level*, from a Greek word for nourishment.

When anything dies, from a leaf to a bison, a third group takes over. *Decomposers* such as fungi and bacteria break dead tissue into simple substances: carbon dioxide, water, and minerals that plants can take up again. Without them the prairie would be buried under centuries of dead grass, and the nutrients locked in that grass would never return to the soil. Under the site's microscope, a pinch of leaf litter in water shows this crew at work.

Notice the difference between energy and matter here. Matter cycles: a carbon atom in a grass blade can pass through a grasshopper, a bird, a fungus and back into the air. Energy does not cycle. It flows in as sunlight, passes from level to level, and leaves as heat. The sun must keep shining or the whole system runs down.

words.d: an organism that makes its own food from sunlight or chemicals, such as a plant or an alga
an organism that gets its energy by eating other organisms
an organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks dead matter into simple substances plants can reuse
a feeding position in an ecosystem, such as producer, herbivore or top predator

look.title: One Square Meter of Prairie
look.text: Mark off one square meter of prairie or lawn with string. Inside it you find grasses, clover, a dandelion, two ants, a beetle, a spider, a worm and some rotting leaves covered in white threads of fungus.
look.prompt: Sort everything you found into producers, consumers and decomposers. Which group has the most living things, and why?

check.q: Which organism is a producer?
choices: A mushroom on a rotting log
Big bluestem grass
A grasshopper
A red-tailed hawk
check.why: Grass makes its own food by photosynthesis. The mushroom is a decomposer; the grasshopper and hawk are consumers.

check.q: What would happen to a forest if all decomposers vanished?
choices: Plants would grow faster
Dead matter would pile up and nutrients would stay locked inside it
Consumers would become producers
The forest would receive more sunlight
check.why: Decomposers return minerals from dead tissue to the soil. Without them, nutrients would never be recycled.

check.q: Which statement about energy and matter in an ecosystem is correct?
choices: Both energy and matter cycle endlessly
Energy cycles but matter flows through once
Neither energy nor matter moves between organisms
Matter cycles, but energy flows through and leaves as heat
check.why: Atoms are reused again and again, but energy enters as sunlight and is lost as heat at every step.

lessons.title: The Ten Percent Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level is stored in the bodies of the next level up, which is why food chains are short and top predators are rare.
reading: Why are there so many grasshoppers in a prairie and so few hawks? Count them and the difference is enormous. Weigh them and it is still huge. The reason is energy. When a grasshopper eats a leaf, most of the leaf's energy does not become grasshopper. Some passes out undigested. Most is burned to keep the insect moving, growing and warm, and leaves as heat. Only a small share is stored in new grasshopper tissue that a bird could eat.

Ecologists measured this in lakes and fields. As a rough average, about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level ends up stored in the next. This is the *ten percent rule*. Suppose a patch of prairie stores 10,000 kilocalories of sunlight energy in its plants during a season. Roughly 1,000 will end up in herbivores. About 100 will reach the animals that eat herbivores, and about 10 the top predators. The real share ranges from a few percent to around 20, but 10 is a fair rule of thumb.

Stack the trophic levels and you get an *energy pyramid*, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. The pyramid explains why food chains rarely run past four or five links. By the fifth level there is not enough energy left to feed a population. It also explains why a wolf pack needs a territory of many square miles while the elk it hunts need far less. And it explains why farming grain feeds more people per acre than farming beef.

The pyramid is about energy, not necessarily numbers or weight. A single oak tree can feed thousands of caterpillars, so a pyramid of numbers may look upside down at the base. In the ocean, tiny algae reproduce so fast that a small standing crop of them supports a heavier crop of animals. But an energy pyramid, measured over a whole season, is always wide at the bottom.

words.d: the rough rule that only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is stored in the next level up
a diagram of trophic levels stacked by the energy each holds, wide at the producers and narrow at the top predators
a unit of energy; the food Calorie on a nutrition label is one kilocalorie

look.title: Energy Left at Each Level
look.cite: standard ten percent rule, illustrative values
look.prompt: Where did the other 9,000 kilocalories go between the grasses and the grasshoppers? How many kilocalories of grass would it take to support a single fourth-level consumer?

check.q: About what share of a trophic level's energy is stored in the next level up?
choices: About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 90 percent
All of it
check.why: The ten percent rule: roughly a tenth is stored; the rest is lost as heat, used for living, or left undigested.

check.q: Where does most of the energy a grasshopper eats end up?
choices: Stored in its body for a bird to eat
Released as heat after powering its life processes
Returned to the grass
Stored in the soil
check.why: Most consumed energy is used for movement, growth and warmth and leaves as heat; only a small share becomes new tissue.

check.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than five links?
choices: Animals refuse to eat predators
Top predators are too fast to catch
Too little energy remains after several transfers to support another level
Producers stop making food after five links
check.why: Each transfer loses about 90 percent of the energy, so after a few levels there is not enough left to feed a population.

lessons.title: Food Webs, Not Chains
lessons.mainIdea: Real ecosystems are food webs in which most species eat and are eaten by several others, so a change in one population ripples through many.
reading: A food chain is a tidy line: grass to grasshopper to meadowlark to hawk. Real prairies are not tidy. The hawk also eats mice, snakes and rabbits. The meadowlark also eats beetles and seeds. The grasshopper is also eaten by spiders, toads and ground squirrels. Draw every arrow and you get a *food web*, a tangle of feeding links that looks more like a fishing net than a chain.

Webs matter because they change what happens when a population rises or falls. In a simple chain, losing the grasshoppers would starve the meadowlarks. In a web, the meadowlarks switch to beetles. That flexibility makes a diverse ecosystem more *stable*: it can absorb a shock without collapsing. A field with only one crop and one pest is a chain, and it is fragile.

Webs also carry effects in surprising directions. When wolves returned to Yellowstone, they killed elk, and leftover carcasses fed ravens, eagles, magpies and bears through the winter. Coyote numbers dropped because wolves kill coyotes, and with fewer coyotes, more pronghorn fawns survived. None of that appears in a chain that reads wolf to elk to willow.

Ecologists map food webs by watching who eats whom, by examining stomach contents and droppings, and by tracing chemical markers through tissue. The maps are never finished, because feeding changes with the season and the year. But even a partial map lets you make a prediction and then test it, which is the whole point of drawing one.

words.d: a diagram of all the feeding links in an ecosystem, showing that most species eat and are eaten by several others
able to absorb a disturbance without changing greatly or collapsing
a single line of who eats whom, from producer to top consumer

look.title: A Web With One Thread Cut
look.text: A prairie food web has grasses, grasshoppers, beetles, mice, meadowlarks, snakes and a pair of hawks. One summer a new insect disease wipes out nearly all the grasshoppers. The meadowlarks, which ate mostly grasshoppers, are thin for a while but survive on beetles. The snakes, which ate mostly mice, are unaffected. The hawks do fine.
look.prompt: Redraw this scene as a simple chain instead of a web. What would have happened to the meadowlarks? What does that tell you about diversity and stability?

check.q: Which best describes a food web?
choices: A single line from producer to top predator
A diagram of an energy pyramid
A list of producers only
A tangle of many feeding links among the species of an ecosystem
check.why: A food web shows that most species have several food sources and several predators, unlike a single chain.

check.q: Why can a diverse food web absorb the loss of one prey species better than a simple chain can?
choices: Consumers can switch to other prey
Diverse webs have no predators
Producers make more food in a web
Decomposers stop working in chains
check.why: When a consumer has several food sources, losing one does not starve it, so the shock does not spread as far.

check.q: After wolves returned to Yellowstone, pronghorn fawns survived better. Which link in the web best explains this?
choices: Wolves ate the grass that pronghorn needed
Wolves reduced coyotes, which had been eating fawns
Wolves protected the fawns from eagles
Wolves made the elk eat less willow
check.why: Wolves kill coyotes, coyotes prey on pronghorn fawns, so fewer coyotes meant more fawns survived.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: Water moves in an endless cycle among ocean, air, land and living things, driven by the sun and gravity, and every organism depends on that flow.
reading: A puddle on a Chicago sidewalk vanishes by afternoon. It did not disappear. The sun's energy turned it into vapor that drifted upward, perhaps to cool and condense into a cloud over Lake Michigan, perhaps to fall as rain in Indiana by nightfall. Water on Earth is old and endlessly reused. The glass you drink today may hold molecules that once fell on a dinosaur.

The *water cycle* has a few main moves. *Evaporation* lifts water from oceans, lakes and soil into the air as vapor. Plants add to it through *transpiration*, pulling water up from their roots and releasing it through pores in their leaves; a single large tree can release hundreds of liters on a hot day. High in the air, vapor cools and condenses into droplets, forming clouds. Precipitation, as rain or snow, returns it to the surface. Then gravity takes over: water runs off into streams or soaks into the ground to become groundwater.

Almost all of Earth's water, roughly 97 percent, is salty ocean. Most of the fresh water is locked in ice sheets and glaciers. The lakes, rivers and shallow groundwater that ecosystems and cities actually use are a tiny fraction of the total. That is why the Great Lakes, holding about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water, are such a treasure.

Living things are part of the cycle, not spectators. Prairie roots slow runoff and let rain soak in, recharging groundwater. Forests pump vast amounts of vapor into the air, feeding rain downwind. Pave a watershed and rain rushes off in hours, flooding streams and skipping the ground entirely. That is one reason Chicago builds rain gardens and permeable pavement.

words.d: the continuous movement of water among ocean, air, land and living things
the change of liquid water into water vapor, driven by heat
the release of water vapor from plant leaves
water that has soaked into the ground and fills spaces in soil and rock

look.title: Where Earth's Water Is
rows: Groundwater, lakes, rivers, air and living things
look.prompt: If almost all fresh water is frozen, what fraction of Earth's water is actually available to a prairie stream or a city? Why does that matter for how we treat it?

check.q: What supplies the energy that lifts water from a lake into the air?
choices: Gravity
Wind alone
The sun
Plant roots
check.why: Solar energy drives evaporation. Gravity is what brings water back down as rain and runoff.

check.q: How do plants add water to the air?
choices: By condensation in their roots
By freezing water in their stems
By absorbing rain directly into the sky
By transpiration through pores in their leaves
check.why: Plants pull water up from the soil and release it as vapor through leaf pores.

check.q: A town paves over a prairie. What most likely happens to rainwater there?
choices: More of it runs off quickly into streams and less soaks into the ground
More of it soaks into the ground
It evaporates before it lands
It is absorbed by the pavement
check.why: Pavement blocks infiltration, so rain rushes off as surface runoff instead of recharging groundwater.

lessons.title: The Carbon Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: Carbon atoms cycle between air, living things, soil, ocean and rock; burning fossil fuels adds carbon to the air faster than the cycle removes it.
reading: Take a breath. The carbon dioxide you exhale was, a few hours ago, part of your breakfast. Before that it was part of a wheat plant, and before that it was carbon dioxide in the air that the plant pulled in through its leaves. Carbon is the backbone of every living molecule, and it rides a loop called the *carbon cycle* that passes through you.

The fast part of the loop runs through living things. *Photosynthesis* pulls carbon dioxide out of the air and builds it into sugar. Respiration, in plants, animals and decomposers, burns that sugar and returns carbon dioxide to the air. The ocean joins in too: carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater, where algae take it up and shells and sediments store some of it. This exchange moves enormous amounts of carbon every year in both directions, roughly in balance.

The slow part of the loop is buried. Over millions of years, some dead plants and algae were buried and squeezed into coal, oil and natural gas, the *fossil fuels*. That carbon sat underground, out of the cycle. Since the 1800s, people have been digging it up and burning it, which sends carbon dioxide into the air far faster than photosynthesis, the oceans and rock weathering can pull it back out.

Scientists have measured the result directly. On Mauna Loa in Hawaii, an observatory has sampled the air since 1958. The carbon dioxide level was about 315 parts per million then; it passed 420 parts per million in the 2020s. Every year the line wobbles, dipping in the Northern Hemisphere summer as forests leaf out and rising in winter, a global breath drawn on a graph. The long-term rise, though, points only one way, and it is the main driver of the warming climate.

words.d: the movement of carbon atoms among the air, living things, soil, ocean and rock
the process by which plants and algae use light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water
coal, oil or natural gas, formed from living things buried millions of years ago
a unit for tiny concentrations: 420 parts per million means 420 molecules out of every million

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa
look.prompt: By roughly how much did the level rise in each 20-year span? Is the rise speeding up, slowing down, or steady?

check.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
choices: Respiration
Photosynthesis
Burning coal
Decomposition
check.why: Photosynthesis builds carbon dioxide into sugar. The other three all release carbon dioxide.

check.q: Why does burning fossil fuels change the carbon cycle?
choices: It stops photosynthesis
It removes carbon from the ocean
It releases carbon that had been buried out of the cycle for millions of years
It turns carbon into a different element
check.why: Fossil carbon was stored underground. Burning it adds carbon dioxide faster than natural processes can remove it.

check.q: The Mauna Loa record dips a little every summer. What best explains the dip?
choices: Volcanoes stop erupting in summer
Oceans freeze in summer
People burn less fuel on hot days
Northern forests leaf out and pull in carbon dioxide
check.why: Most land plants are in the Northern Hemisphere; their summer growth draws down carbon dioxide for a few months.

lessons.title: The Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: Nitrogen is plentiful in the air but useless to most life until bacteria fix it into usable forms, and human fertilizer now adds as much as nature does.
reading: Every protein in your body and every strand of DNA needs nitrogen. The air is about 78 percent nitrogen gas, so you might expect no shortage. But nitrogen gas is two atoms bonded so tightly that plants and animals cannot pull them apart. For most of life, the nitrogen in the air is like ocean water to a thirsty sailor: everywhere and unusable.

The key is a small group of *bacteria* that can break that bond. They perform *nitrogen fixation*, turning nitrogen gas into ammonia and related compounds that plants can absorb. Some live free in soil and water; others live inside lumps on the roots of legumes such as clover, soybeans and prairie plants like leadplant. Lightning fixes a little too. Once fixed, nitrogen passes from plant to animal to decomposer and back into the soil, and other bacteria eventually return it to the air as gas, closing the *nitrogen cycle*.

For thousands of years, fixation set a ceiling on how much food a farm could grow. Then in the early 1900s the German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch found a way to make ammonia from air and hydrogen in a factory. That invention became synthetic *fertilizer*, and today it helps feed roughly half the world's people. People now fix about as much nitrogen each year as all natural processes combined.

The cost shows up downstream. Nitrogen that plants do not use washes off fields into rivers. In the Mississippi basin, which drains most of Illinois, that runoff feeds algae blooms in the Gulf of Mexico. When the algae die and decompose, bacteria use up the oxygen, creating a summer dead zone covering thousands of square miles where fish and shrimp cannot live. Farmers, scientists and towns are testing cover crops, buffer strips and wetlands to hold nitrogen on the land.

words.d: the change of nitrogen gas from the air into forms such as ammonia that plants can use
single-celled organisms, some of which fix nitrogen or decompose dead matter
the movement of nitrogen among the air, soil, water and living things
a substance added to soil to supply nutrients such as nitrogen for plant growth

look.title: The Lumps on the Clover Root
look.text: Pull up a clover plant from a lawn and rinse the roots. You will find small pink or white lumps, each the size of a pinhead. Inside each lump live millions of bacteria. The clover gives them sugar; they give the clover usable nitrogen. Farmers in Illinois rotate soybeans, a legume, with corn partly because the soybean roots leave nitrogen behind in the soil.
look.prompt: Why would a farmer plant soybeans one year and corn the next instead of corn every year? What does each partner in the root lump gain?

check.q: Why can most plants not use the nitrogen gas in the air?
choices: The two nitrogen atoms are bonded too tightly for plants to break apart
There is not enough nitrogen in the air
Nitrogen gas is poisonous to plants
Plants have no way to touch the air
check.why: Nitrogen gas is very stable. Only certain bacteria, lightning and factories can split it into usable forms.

check.q: Which organisms carry out most nitrogen fixation in nature?
choices: Earthworms
Certain bacteria
Fungi
Grasses
check.why: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, some living in legume root nodules, convert nitrogen gas into ammonia.

check.q: How does nitrogen fertilizer in Illinois help create a dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico?
choices: It poisons fish directly
It makes the Gulf too salty
Runoff feeds algae blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen in the water
It blocks sunlight from reaching the Gulf
check.why: Excess nitrogen fuels algae growth; when the algae die, decomposers consume the oxygen, leaving too little for fish.

lessons.title: Competition, Predation, Symbiosis
lessons.mainIdea: Species interact by competing for resources, by eating one another, and by living closely together in ways that help, harm or barely affect their partners.
reading: No species lives alone. Every population is pushed and pulled by others around it, and ecologists sort those interactions into a few types. *Competition* happens when two individuals or species need the same limited resource: light, water, food, nesting holes. Gause's paramecia showed it clearly. Two species grown together in one tube could not both hold on; one always crowded the other out. Two species that need exactly the same things cannot share the same place for long.

*Predation* is one organism eating another. It shapes both sides. Prey rely on speed, camouflage, armor and alarm calls; predators rely on sharp senses and teamwork. The snowshoe hare and the lynx rise and fall together. Herbivory, a plant being eaten, works the same way, which is why prairie plants bristle with silica, thorns and bitter chemicals.

*Symbiosis* means two species living in close, long-term contact. It comes in three flavors. In mutualism both gain: the clover and its root bacteria, the bee and the flower it pollinates. In commensalism one gains and the other is unaffected: a bird nesting in a tree. In parasitism one gains and the other is harmed but usually not killed outright: a tick on a deer, a tapeworm in a gut.

These interactions are not fixed facts about a species. They are relationships that shift with conditions. A fungus that helps a tree's roots find water in dry soil may take more than it gives in a wet year. The point of naming the types is to make a prediction you can test. If you remove this partner, what happens to that one?

words.d: an interaction in which two organisms or species need the same limited resource
an interaction in which one organism eats another
a close, long-term relationship between two species; it may help both, one, or harm one
a symbiosis in which both partners benefit

look.title: Malthus on Growth and Food
look.text: Malthus argued that a human population, when nothing checks it, doubles again and again, growing far faster than the food supply, which can only be increased by a fixed amount at a time. Something, he said, must therefore always hold population back, whether hunger, disease or restraint.
look.cite: Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Malthus says a population grows faster than its food. Which limits in this chapter keep an animal population in check?

check.q: Two bird species need the same tree cavities for nesting, and there are few cavities. This interaction is
choices: mutualism
commensalism
parasitism
competition
check.why: Both species need the same limited resource, which is the definition of competition.

check.q: Which relationship is a mutualism?
choices: A bee gathering nectar and pollinating the flower
A tick feeding on a deer
A lynx catching a hare
A tapeworm living in a dog's gut
check.why: Both the bee and the flower benefit. The tick and tapeworm are parasites; the lynx is a predator.

check.q: Gause grew two paramecium species that needed the same food in one tube, and one species always died out. What does this show?
choices: Paramecia are parasites
Two species with identical needs cannot share a place for long
Predators always win
Symbiosis is rare in test tubes
check.why: This is the competitive exclusion principle: complete competitors cannot coexist.

lessons.title: Succession After Disturbance
lessons.mainIdea: After a disturbance, a community rebuilds in a roughly predictable sequence called succession, from hardy pioneers toward a longer-lasting mix of species.
reading: On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington blew out its north side and buried hundreds of square miles under ash, mud and blasted trees. Within weeks, scientists walking the gray plain found a purple lupine flowering in the ash. Lupines fix nitrogen, so they could grow where nothing else could, and where they died they left richer soil. Insects arrived, then grasses, then willows and alders. Forty years later, young forest was returning.

Ecologists call this rebuilding *succession*. It begins with a *disturbance*: a fire, a flood, a plowed field abandoned, a glacier melting back. The first arrivals are *pioneer species*, tough plants and animals that tolerate harsh, open conditions and spread quickly. They change the place, adding soil, shade and moisture, which lets other species in. Each stage sets up the next.

There are two kinds. Primary succession starts on bare rock or fresh ash with no soil at all, as on a new lava flow. It can take centuries. Secondary succession starts where soil already exists, such as a burned prairie or a cleared woodlot. It moves much faster. An abandoned Illinois field is thick with weeds the first year and has saplings within a decade.

In 1899 Henry Chandler Cowles of the University of Chicago studied the sand dunes along Lake Michigan in Indiana. Walking inland from the beach, he passed grasses, then shrubs, then pines, then oak forest, each older than the last. He realized he was walking through time: the dunes showed every stage of succession side by side. Later ecologists learned that succession does not always end at one fixed 'climax'; disturbances keep resetting it, and chance matters. But Cowles's walk through time still shapes how ecologists read a landscape.

words.d: the gradual, roughly predictable change in a community's species after a disturbance
an event, such as fire, flood or plowing, that removes organisms and opens space
the first hardy organisms to colonize a disturbed or bare place

look.title: Walking Inland From the Beach
look.text: Stand on a Lake Michigan beach in Indiana and walk straight away from the water. First, bare sand and a few grasses whose roots hold the dune. Then low shrubs, then cottonwoods, then pines with a thin layer of needles underfoot. Farther in, oaks and hickories over dark soil, then in the wettest hollows, maples and beeches. The farther you walk, the older the ground.
look.prompt: Why would the oldest, most sheltered dune carry the biggest trees? What would you expect to find on the same spot the beach grasses occupy today, two hundred years from now?

check.q: Why could lupines grow on the bare ash of Mount St. Helens when other plants could not?
choices: They need no water
They are the tallest plants
They fix nitrogen and tolerate harsh, open conditions
They were planted by scientists
check.why: Lupines are pioneer species; their nitrogen-fixing partners let them thrive on nutrient-poor ash.

check.q: Which situation is secondary succession?
choices: Lichens growing on a fresh lava flow
Moss on rock exposed by a melting glacier
Sand forming on a brand-new dune
Weeds and saplings filling an abandoned cornfield
check.why: Secondary succession starts where soil already exists, such as an old field, and moves faster than primary succession.

check.q: What did Cowles conclude from walking inland across the Indiana dunes?
choices: Each older dune showed a later stage of the same succession
Oaks cannot grow near lakes
Sand dunes never change
Pines are pioneer species
check.why: The dunes farther from the lake were older, so their communities showed later stages of succession side by side.

lessons.title: Keystones and the Prairie Fire
lessons.mainIdea: Some species and some disturbances hold a whole community in shape; remove a keystone species or stop the prairie fires and the community changes completely.
reading: In the 1960s the ecologist Robert Paine spent his summers on the rocky shore of Washington State pulling starfish off the rocks and throwing them into the sea. In the plots where he removed them, mussels, which the starfish ate, spread over everything. Within a few years the number of species in those plots had dropped by about half. One predator, not especially common, had been holding the whole community open. Paine called it a *keystone species*, after the stone at the top of an arch that keeps the rest from falling.

Keystones are not always big predators. Prairie dogs dig burrows that shelter dozens of other animals and clip grass that keeps the plain open. Beavers build dams that create wetlands. Sea otters eat sea urchins that would otherwise mow down kelp forests. What makes a keystone is not size but leverage: its effect on the community is far larger than its numbers suggest. Yellowstone's wolves are a debated example, which is why scientists there keep measuring.

On the Illinois prairie, the keystone was not a species but a *disturbance*. Before settlement, fires set by lightning and by Native peoples swept the tallgrass every few years. Prairie grasses survive because their growing points and most of their mass are underground, in roots that can reach several feet deep. Trees and shrubs, with buds above ground, are killed back. Stop the fires and within a few decades a prairie turns to brush, then woodland.

Illinois calls itself the Prairie State. Roughly 22 million acres of tallgrass once covered it. Only a tiny fraction of that, well under one percent, survives in scattered remnants. Every remnant and every restoration is burned on purpose by trained crews, from Nachusa Grasslands to small patches in Cook County forest preserves. Watch one of those spring burns. You are seeing a community held in shape by the very thing that looks like its destruction.

words.d: a species whose effect on its community is far larger than its numbers would suggest
an event, such as fire, that removes organisms and opens space; some communities depend on it
the grassland of deep-rooted grasses and wildflowers that once covered most of Illinois
a small surviving piece of an original habitat that was never plowed or built on

look.title: Paine and the Missing Starfish
look.text: Paine reported that in the shoreline plots where he kept removing the starfish Pisaster, mussels took over the rock and crowded out most of the other species. The plots with the starfish stayed diverse. He concluded that a single predator could control the makeup of a whole community.
look.prompt: Why was removing the starfish, rather than just counting them, the key step in this experiment? Design a similar test for a prairie species.

check.q: What happened in the plots where Paine removed the starfish?
choices: More species moved in
Mussels took over and the number of species dropped
The starfish came back stronger
Nothing changed
check.why: Without their predator, mussels crowded out other species, cutting diversity roughly in half.

check.q: Why do prairie grasses survive a fire that kills young trees?
choices: Grass leaves are fireproof
Fire never reaches the ground in a prairie
Their growing points and most of their mass are underground
They grow back from seeds carried by wind
check.why: Grasses regrow from buds and deep roots below the soil, while tree buds above ground are killed by the flames.

check.q: What would you predict for a prairie remnant that is never burned?
choices: It will stay prairie forever
It will become desert
It will grow more wildflowers each year
It will turn to brush and then woodland within decades
check.why: Without fire, shrubs and trees invade and shade out the grasses; fire is the disturbance that keeps prairie open.

review.q: A population's growth graph is J-shaped. Which is most likely true?
choices: Limiting factors have not yet slowed it
It has reached carrying capacity
It is being controlled by disease
It is shrinking
review.why: A J-shaped curve is exponential growth, which happens only while resources are still plentiful.

review.q: Which is a density-independent limiting factor?
choices: Food shortage in a crowded herd
A flash flood
A parasite spreading in a dense colony
Competition for nesting sites
review.why: A flood strikes regardless of how many individuals live there; the others depend on crowding.

review.q: Why does an ecosystem need a constant input of sunlight but not a constant input of carbon?
choices: Carbon is not needed by living things
Sunlight is stored forever in plants
Energy flows through and is lost as heat, while carbon atoms cycle and are reused
Carbon comes from the sun
review.why: Matter cycles; energy does not. Each transfer loses energy as heat, so it must be replaced.

review.q: A prairie stores 50,000 kilocalories in its plants. About how much would you expect in its secondary consumers?
review.why: Apply the ten percent rule twice: 50,000 to 5,000 in herbivores, then 5,000 to 500 in secondary consumers.

review.q: Which process returns carbon dioxide to the air?
choices: Respiration by decomposers
Photosynthesis
Nitrogen fixation
Transpiration
review.why: Respiration, in any organism, releases carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis removes it.

review.q: Legumes are useful to farmers mainly because
choices: their roots hold water
bacteria in their roots fix nitrogen into the soil
they never need sunlight
they repel all insects
review.why: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules leave usable nitrogen behind, reducing the need for fertilizer.

review.q: A fungus on a tree's roots takes sugar from the tree and helps the roots gather water. When both benefit, this is
choices: parasitism
predation
mutualism
competition
review.why: Mutualism is a symbiosis in which both partners gain.

review.q: A Cook County prairie remnant has not been burned in thirty years. What has most likely happened, and why?
choices: It is richer in wildflowers, because fire kills seeds
It has turned to bare soil, because grass cannot live without fire
It is unchanged, because prairie is a stable climax
It has filled with shrubs and trees, because fire was the disturbance that kept them out
review.why: Prairie depends on periodic fire; without it, woody plants with above-ground buds invade and shade out the grasses.
